canonicalExplanation.summary: When several controls answer **one question** — radio buttons, related checkboxes, the parts of an address — wrap them in `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>` that asks the question. Each option still needs its own label. Radios share one `name` so only one can be chosen. The `autocomplete` attribute (`name`, `email`, `postal-code`…) tells browsers what each field is for, so they can fill it in correctly.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A checkout asks for delivery: three radio buttons labelled "Standard", "Express", "Pickup". A screen-reader user tabs to one and hears "Express, radio button, 2 of 3" — Express what? Delivery? Payment? A delivery-method fieldset uses legend Delivery method and labels each radio option. In this lesson you'll group related choices and configure input purpose without relying on placeholder labels.

```predict
{"question": "Three radios share `name=\"delivery\"`. How many can be selected at once?", "options": ["All three", "One"], "answer": 1, "why": "Radios with the same name form one group: selecting one deselects the others, and only that value is submitted."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Paragraph and inline meaning**, **Relative and absolute URLs**, and **Labels and input controls** — every option needs its own label.

sections.heading: The model: fieldset asks, legend names, labels answer
sections.body:
```html
<fieldset>
  <legend>Delivery method</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="delivery" value="standard" checked> Standard (3–5 days)</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="delivery" value="express"> Express (next day)</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="delivery" value="pickup"> Pickup from store</label>
</fieldset>

<fieldset>
  <legend>Shipping address</legend>
  <label for="street">Street</label>
  <input id="street" name="street" autocomplete="street-address">
  <label for="pin">PIN code</label>
  <input id="pin" name="pin" autocomplete="postal-code" inputmode="numeric">
</fieldset>
```

| Piece | Job |
|---|---|
| `fieldset`. | groups controls that answer one question. |
| `legend`. | the question, announced with each option. |
| shared radio `name`. | one choice per group. |
| `autocomplete`. | tells the browser the field's purpose. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Does a single text field need a fieldset?", "answer": "No. A lone control just needs its label. Use fieldset when several controls share a question."}
```

sections.heading: Purpose, not placeholders

includes: Group related radios, checkboxes and multi-part fields with fieldset and legend.
Set autocomplete tokens to declare each field's purpose.

outcomes: Group related choices and configure input purpose without relying on placeholder labels.

examples.title: Choosing a delivery method
examples.situation: A delivery-method fieldset uses legend Delivery method and labels each radio option.
walkthrough: **Fieldset with legend Delivery method:** names the question for the whole group.
**Labels each radio option:** Standard, Express and Pickup each have their own label, and share `name="delivery"`.
**Result:** a screen reader will read "Delivery method, Express (next day), radio button, 2 of 3".
examples.result: Every option is announced with its question, and only one delivery method can be chosen.

examples.title: The address form without purpose
examples.situation: An address form has fields named f1–f5 with placeholders only; the browser autofills a phone number into the PIN code box.
walkthrough: The browser couldn't tell what each field was for.
Placeholders vanished while typing, and no labels named the fields.
Fix: labels for each field, a fieldset with legend Shipping address, and autocomplete tokens like `postal-code`.
examples.result: Autofill puts the right values in the right boxes, and each field is clearly named.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Radio buttons with the same name never need a group label.
misconceptions.correction: A shared name only makes the options mutually exclusive; it doesn't name the question. Without a fieldset and legend, users hear options like "Express" without knowing what they're choosing.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "Choosing a delivery method", what does the legend add to each option's announcement?

analogy.example: A fieldset is like a **question on a paper survey** with tick boxes under it: the question (legend) makes sense of the answers (labels). autocomplete is like writing "for office use: postcode" next to a box so the clerk knows what goes there.
limitations: Paper surveys can't enforce one choice; shared radio names do.
Browsers can fill fields for you only if purpose is declared.

remediation.explanation: For every set of controls ask: **Do they answer one shared question?** Yes → fieldset + legend. Then for each text field: **what personal data is this?** → matching autocomplete token.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The address form without purpose".

recap.summary: To group related choices, wrap them in fieldset with a legend stating the question and label every option; radios in one group share a name. Configure input purpose with autocomplete tokens instead of relying on placeholder labels.
